---
{"publish":true,"title":"Disjoint Memory Schemes","tags":["CS2106","memory","operating_systems"],"PassFrontmatter":true}
---

Previously, two assumptions:
- each process occupies a contiguous memory region ❌
- physical memory is large enough to contain one or more processes with complete memory space

Assuming the first assumption is not made, we can use the **paging scheme**.

# General Idea

The
- **physical memory** is split into regions of fixed size (**physical frame**)
- **logical memory** is split into regions of same size (**logical page**)

At execution time, pages of a process are loaded into any available memory frame:
- logical memory space remains contiguous
- occupied physical memory region can be disjoined

> [!pros] This allows for a lot flexibility, as the occupied physical memory does not have to follow the continuity as intended.

# Page Table

In contiguous memory allocation, usage of a process is tracked simply (starting address, size of process).

However, with **paging scheme**:
- mapping between logical page and physical frame
- a lookup table is needed

## Logical Address

> [!important] Design decisions
> - Frame size is a power-of-2
> - Physical frame size == Logical frame size

$$
\text{Physical address} = \text{Frame size} \times \text{Frame number} + \text{Offset}
$$

12.600000000000001)"><text x="103.5499267578125" y="20" font-family="Local Font, Segoe UI Emoji" font-size="20px" fill="#1e1e1e" text-anchor="middle" style="white-space: pre;" direction="ltr" dominant-baseline="alphabetic">translation mechanism</text></g></svg>


Given
- page/frame size of $2^{n}$
- $m$ bits of logical address,

the formula is as follows:

$$
\begin{equation}
\text{Physical address} = f \times 2^{n} + d
\end{equation}
$$

where
- $p$ refers to the most significant $m-n$ bits of $\text{Logical address}$
- $d$ refers to the remaining $n$ bits of the $\text{Logical address}$
- $f$ refers to the frame number, which is found from using mapping mechanism (such as page table) on $p$

<u>Step-by-step</u>:

1. Find the page size in bytes.
	- for example, 4 bytes.
2. Find how many bits needed for the offset $d$. This is $\log_{2}\text{page\_size}$
	- $d = 2$
3. Determine how many pages there are.
	- there are 4 logical pages
4. Determine $p$, $log_{2}(\text{no. of logical pages})$, which is the number of bits for the page number.
	- $p = 2$
5. Determine how many frames there are.
	- there are 8 physical frames
6. Determine $f$, $log_{2}(\text{no. of physical frames})$, which is the number of bits for the page number.
	- $p = 3$

> [!pros] 
> - No external fragmentation
> - Very less internal fragmentation
> 	- generally only last frame
> - Clear separation of logical and physical address space
> 	- allows for great flexibility
> 	- simple address translation

## Implementation

### Pure-Software Solution

OS stores page table information in PCB - thus the page table is the **memory context** of a process.

> [!cons] Require two memory access for each memory reference
> - first reference to get the page table for the process
> - second to get the actual offset for that process

Possible fixes for this - **caching**

### Hardware Support

> [!note] Translation Look-Aside Buffer (TLB)
> TLB acts as a cache of a few page table entries.

Logical address translation with **TLB**
- **TLB-Hit**: entry is found - frame number retrieved to generate physical address
- **TLB-Miss**: entry is not found - memory access is needed to access the full page table, and retrieved frame number is used to generate physical address and update TLB

style="white-space: pre;" direction="ltr" dominant-baseline="alphabetic">TLB</text></g></svg>

To calculate the impact on memory access time, consider
- time taken for TLB access ${tlb}$
- time taken for main memory access $\text{mem}$
- percentage of page table contained in TLB $\text{per}$

The memory access time is thus

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Memory access time} &= \bbox[lightgreen, 2pt]{\color{black} \text{TLB hit}} + \bbox[pink, 2pt]{\color{black} \text{TLB miss}} \\
&= \bbox[lightgreen, 2pt]{\color{black} \text{per} \times (\text{tlb} +\text{mem})} + \bbox[pink, 2pt]{\color{black} (1 - \text{per}) \times (\text{tlb} +2 \times \text{mem})} \\
\end{aligned}
$$
When there is a $\bbox[lightgreen, 2pt]{\color{black} \text{TLB hit}}$,
- the time taken is $\text{tlb}$ to access the frame number and the $\text{mem}$ to access the memory itself.

When there is a $\bbox[pink, 2pt]{\color{black} \text{TLB miss}}$,
- the time taken is $\text{tlb}$ to access the frame number, and since there is a miss, $\text{mem}$ to access the page table of the process, and $\text{mem}$ again to access the actual memory.

> [!example] If TLB access takes 1ns, and main memory access takes 50ns, what is the average memory access time if TLB contains 40% of the whole page table?
> 
> $$
> \begin{aligned}
> \text{Memory access time} &= \bbox[lightgreen, 2pt]{\color{black} \text{TLB hit}} + \bbox[pink, 2pt]{\color{black} \text{TLB miss}} \\
> &= \bbox[lightgreen, 2pt]{\color{black} \text{per} \times (\text{tlb} +\text{mem})} + \bbox[pink, 2pt]{\color{black} (1 - \text{per}) \times (\text{tlb} +2 \times \text{mem})} \\
> &= \bbox[lightgreen, 2pt]{\color{black} 40\% \times (1 + 50)\text{ns}} + \bbox[pink, 2pt]{\color{black} 60\% \times (1 + 50 + 50)\text{ns}} \\
> &= 81\text{ns}
> \end{aligned}
> $$

As TLB is part of the **hardware context**
- when a context switch occurs, TLB entries are flushed.
- when a process resumes running, many TLB misses will happen to fill TLB

### Protection

#### Access-Right Bits

By adding bits to specify for each page table entry `writable, readable, executable`, memory access will be checked against the access-right bits.

#### Valid Bit

A valid bit indicates if the page is valid to access.
- some pages are out of range for particular process
- OS will set valid bits when process is running
- out-of-range access will be caught by the OS

### Page sharing

Page tables can allow several processes to share the same physical memory frame 
- the same physical frame number in the page table entries

> [!example] Possible usages
> - Shared code pages (shared standard library, system calls)
> - Copy-On-Write (share the page, until one changes the value in it)
